claims.statement: `createDeepAgent` always installs synchronous subagent middleware and adds the async subagent bridge only when its unified `subagents` collection contains an `AsyncSubAgent`, identified by the presence of `graphId`.

Synchronous delegation is exposed through a `task` tool that selects a named subagent and invokes either a compiled runnable or a declarative specification, while duplicate names and unknown subagent types are rejected.
A `CompiledSubAgent` bypasses declarative compilation and can wrap a complete deep agent, enabling nested hierarchies in which a child deep agent delegates to its own subagents.

Declarative subagents receive default filesystem, summarization, and tool-call-patching middleware, but custom subagents do not inherit root skills by default; the general-purpose subagent is the exception and inherits the parent model, tools, and skills.

The default synchronous subagent mode is isolated: the child receives only a new human message containing the delegated description, and the child result is returned as a `task` `ToolMessage` plus state filtered to protect parent channels.

The isolated and compiled-subagent state boundary excludes `messages`, `todos`, `structuredResponse`, `skillsMetadata`, `memoryContents`, all four model and tool call-count keys, summarization event and session keys, and the internal fork marker from both inbound and outbound state.

A declarative `mode: "fork"` inherits the parent's effective conversation and prompt-producing state, removes structured-response, call-count, and summarization keys, appends its own system prompt instead of replacing the parent's, and cannot declare its own skills.

Fork execution strips an in-flight parent `AIMessage` with unresolved tool calls, uses the effective summarized history, and refuses a fork's attempt to invoke `task` again instead of allowing recursive delegation.

Model-call and tool-call limit bookkeeping is intentionally excluded at delegation boundaries so each graph owns its own call budget; forwarding those plain single-writer channels can cause concurrent-update failures or a child reset to overwrite the parent's budget.

Subagent filesystem permissions use `input.permissions ?? parentPermissions`: omission inherits the parent rules, `[]` explicitly replaces them with no restrictions, and a non-empty child array fully replaces rather than merges the parent rules.

When a child returns `structuredResponse`, synchronous delegation JSON-serializes it as the parent task `ToolMessage`; otherwise it walks backward to the last non-empty AI message and falls back to `Task completed` when no usable text exists.

An `AsyncSubAgent` targets a remote Agent Protocol graph with `name`, `description`, `graphId`, and optional `url` and headers; clients are cached by URL and resolved headers, with `x-auth-scheme: langsmith` added unless explicitly overridden.

The async middleware provides exactly five tools for starting, checking, updating, cancelling, and listing remote tasks, validates that at least one async agent exists, and rejects duplicate async agent names.

Starting an async task creates a remote thread and run, uses the thread ID as both `taskId` and `threadId`, persists the run as `running` with timestamps, and returns the task ID immediately; a parent thread ID is passed as callback context when available.

Async task status supports `pending`, `running`, `success`, `error`, `cancelled`, `timeout`, and `interrupted`; listing filters cached records first, fetches non-terminal statuses concurrently, skips terminal-status network calls, and falls back to cached status on SDK errors.

Updating an async task creates a new run on the same remote thread with `multitaskStrategy: "interrupt"`, preserving the task ID while replacing the run ID; cancellation calls `runs.cancel` and persists `cancelled`.

Async task records live in a reduced `asyncTasks` state channel keyed by task ID, whose shallow-merging reducer preserves unrelated records while replacing updated entries; checks and lists persist refreshed status and timestamps.

The experimental completion callback middleware sends a completion summary or generic model-error notification to a callback thread via `runs.create`, truncates long final messages and includes a task-ID retrieval hint, while swallowing callback-delivery failures and rethrowing the original model error.
